items.title: 27.3.2 Role of Inhibitors in Enzyme-Catalysed Reactions

source_refs.note: Topic 27.3.2 with the cobra box and the first Quick Check 27.3, answered (PDF 168-169); Figures 27.8 and 27.9 are redrawn in the topic 27.3 figure. Printed slips are corrected in a warning; the book's equating of non-competitive with irreversible is reported as the book's. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Small molecules or ions that cause enzymes to lose their catalytic activity are inhibitors. Different inhibitors act differently, but all stop the active site from binding the substrate.

items: Competitive (reversible) inhibitors have the same shape as the substrate. The substrate and the inhibitor compete for the active site; the more inhibitor, the more the enzyme is deactivated for its substrate. For example, butanedioate (succinate, -OOC-CH2-CH2-COO-) is oxidised by the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase, and propanedioate (malonate, -OOC-CH2-COO-) inhibits this enzyme because it resembles succinate.

Non-competitive inhibitors, which the book treats as irreversible, are small ions or molecules that change the shape of the active site so that it is no longer available to the substrate. An enzyme to which an irreversible inhibitor, such as a poison, an antibiotic, an anti-metabolite or some drugs, is attached loses its activity permanently; such inhibition can cause severe health problems or even death. Penicillin is an irreversible inhibitor of the enzyme transpeptidase, which bacteria need to build their cell walls, so penicillin kills bacteria by disrupting cell wall synthesis.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Cobra venom contains the enzyme phospholipase A2 (PLA2), which can break down the membranes of red blood cells, causing haemolysis, swelling of the affected organ and ultimately death.

blocks.title: Two slips corrected
blocks.text: The book says 'thus insulin kills bacteria' after describing penicillin; it is penicillin that kills bacteria. It also names the enzyme 'dehydrogenase succinate'; the name is succinate dehydrogenase.

blocks.prompt: How do enzymes differ from inorganic catalysts?
blocks.explanation: Enzymes are proteins; they are highly specific (one substrate), very fast, work under mild conditions (about 37 C, near-neutral pH) and are denatured by heat or the wrong pH. Inorganic catalysts are less specific, often need high temperatures and are not denatured.

blocks.prompt: What is the effect of decreasing and of increasing temperature on enzyme activity?
blocks.explanation: Lowering the temperature slows the reaction (fewer, gentler collisions) without destroying the enzyme. Raising it increases activity up to the optimum; above that the enzyme is denatured and activity falls sharply.

A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds the active site, reversibly; adding more substrate can overcome it. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the shape of the active site; more substrate does not overcome it (the book treats these as irreversible).

blocks.prompt: An enzyme is a protein. Explain, in terms of protein structure, how a change in pH disturbs its function.
blocks.explanation: pH changes the charges on acidic and basic side chains (-COOH/-COO-, -NH2/-NH3+). This breaks ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds that hold the tertiary structure, so the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits (the enzyme is denatured).

items: Competitive inhibitors mimic the substrate (malonate for succinate).
Non-competitive inhibitors change the active site; poisons and penicillin act irreversibly.
